blocks.text: For the toad, or the tortoise, has nothing in common with serpents. Such different animals cannot copulate, nor, if they did mate, could some third thing be born from them. Accordingly no one has so far shown what that third species, born of a snake and a toad (or a tortoise), might be. Therefore, however inept the masters of the Hebrews may be, far be it from me to think that they reached such a degree of folly as to invent these monsters. These three words, then, חרדון chardon, חכינא chacina, and חברבר chabarber, certainly designate three animals which, though different in species, nevertheless agree in genus. Nor is it so very difficult to show what they are. For we have already learned that חרדון chardon is the same as צב tsab, or ضب [ḍabb] dhab, a kind of lizard about which the Arabs have taught us so much. And for חכינא chacina we must most certainly read חבינא chabina, with Beth and Caph interchanged; these letters are very similar and are not rarely confused through the carelessness of copyists. Accordingly Buxtorf observes that in the Ialkut this word is read with Beth, חבנא chabna, or chabina, and this spelling is entirely correct. For in Arabic حبن [ḥabana] chabna means to suffer from dropsy. No word is more frequent in the books of the physicians. And hence ام حبين [umm ḥubayn] ummo chubaini, as it were mother of dropsy, and حبينة [ḥubayna] chubaina, or chabina, as it were the dropsical one, is the name of the female chameleon, or of a certain species of lizard very like it, because it has a swollen belly, as if it suffered from dropsy ^{(6)}. Both names are in Alcamus. And the former is explained thus in Damir: واغا سميت بذلك من الحبن لكبر بطنها وهي علي خلقة الحربا غير صدر [wāghā summiyat bi-dhālika min al-ḥabn li-kibar baṭnihā wa-hiya ʿalī khilqat al-ḥirbā ghayr ṣadr] It is so called from dropsy, because of the size of its belly, and it is of the nature of the chameleon, the chest alone excepted. And Ibnossachith: هي اعرض العظاة وراسها عرض [hiya aʿraḍ al-ʿaẓāh wa-raʾsuhā ʿarḍ] This is broader than the common lizard, and has a broad head. And Ibnokatiba: ام حبين تستقبل للشمس [col. 1059] وتدور معها كيف دارت وهذه صفة الحربا [umm ḥubayn tastaqbil lil-shams wa-tadūr maʿahā kayfa dārat wa-hādhihi ṣifat al-ḥirbā] Ummo chubain turns itself toward the sun and turns round with it, which is the property of the chameleon. And the author of المرصع [al-Muraṣṣaʿ], that is, the Inlaid Work: اختلف في ام حبين فقيل هي ضرب من العظا وقيل هي اعرض منها وقيل هي انثي الحرابي يتحاماها الاعراب فلا [II, 481] ياكلونها لنتنها [ukhtulifa fī umm ḥubayn fa-qīla hiya ḍarb min al-ʿaẓā wa-qīla hiya aʿraḍ minhā wa-qīla hiya unthā al-ḥarābī yataḥāmāhā al-aʿrāb fa-lā yaʾkulūnahā li-natnihā] There is disagreement about it. Some say it is a kind of common lizard, others that it is broader, others that it is the female of the chameleon. Because of its stench the Arabs shun it and do not take it as food. This, then, is the chabina, from whose coupling with the chardon the chabarber is imagined to arise, that is, the salamander, if I am not mistaken. How potent its venom is, namely in warmer places, these words of Pliny, book 29, chapter 4, may show: Among all venomous creatures the salamander's wickedness is the greatest. For the others strike individuals and do not kill many at once. The salamander can kill whole peoples unawares. For if it has crept onto a tree, it infects all the fruit with poison and kills those who eat it, with a cold force no different from aconite. Indeed, if a crust of bread is baked on wood it has touched, or with its foot, the same poisoning results, or if it falls into a well. For when its saliva is sprinkled on any part of the body, even the sole of the foot, all the hair on the whole body falls out. And book 10, chapter 67: By its fluid, which it vomits milky from its mouth, whatever part of the human body is touched, all the hair falls out; and the part touched changes its colour into a leprous blotch. And these words of Aelian, book 9, chapter 28, about a pig that has eaten a salamander: Τοὺς γε μὲν αὐτῆς γευσαμένους ἀποκτείνει [Tous ge men autēs geusamenous apokteinei]. It kills those who eat its flesh. And these of Theophrastus: It makes waters with which it has been mixed deadly; likewise fruits, especially when it is dead. And these of Gesner, page 89: Certain Frenchmen once told me that it is commonly said among them that if a Blanda (so the people of Narbonne call the salamander) is found in a heap of wheat, the whole is infected, so much so that even hens feeding on it die. And further on: In certain places of France they call this lizard arressada; they think its bite so deadly that no hope of life remains (which is the very thing the Hebrews say of the chabarber). So they commonly repeat these verses:
Si mordu tá une arressade, Pren ton linceul, et ta flessade.
